activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
story:
Sadie spread the battered paperback open on the kitchen table and set a pad of paper beside it, square and blank as a dare. Her summer assignment was due in eleven days: apply a critical lens to three chapters of a classic novel. She had chosen the lens off a list in the course packet, half because the word "Marxist" looked serious, half because her older cousin Priya, who had taken the same class two years ago, had leaned across the graduation party and said, "Pick that one. It will wreck how you read everything." That sounded like a promise and a warning at once, and Sadie had signed up for both.

The novel she had chosen was Austen, the one everyone claimed to love. On a first pass she had read it the way she read everything, at speed, skating across the surfaces of drawing rooms and errands and proposals. Now the packet told her to slow down and read with a question in her mouth. She found the question in the second page of notes: a Marxist reading often asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible. It told her to notice the servants the novel mentions only in passing. Sadie sat back. She tried to remember a single servant from the whole book and could not.

So she tried something clumsy and literal. She went back to the first chapter she'd flagged and began counting on her fingers, then on paper, making a tally in the margin every time a servant was named. The housekeeper, the cook, a maid dispatched with a note: four times in one chapter, named, useful, folded into the machinery of the day. Then a second tally, for speech. She drew the column and waited for a mark to put in it. She reached the end of the chapter with the column still empty. In an entire chapter of talk, of people explaining themselves at length, no one who worked in that house said a single word on the page.

Her mother came through with a basket of laundry balanced on one hip, saw Sadie's face, and set the basket down. "You look like someone stole something from you."

"In a way." Sadie turned the pad so her mother could see the two columns, one busy, one bare. "The servants in this chapter get named four times. They never talk. Not once." She tapped the empty column. "The whole book is about people who don't have to work, and the people who make that possible are basically furniture."

Her mother pulled out the opposite chair and sat, which she did not usually do in the middle of a laundry run, and Sadie understood that the basket could wait. "Priya would say you're onto something," her mother said. Then, quieter, "When I cleaned rooms at the hotel, the guests talked about me like I was weather. Something that happened to the room." She said it lightly, but she held Sadie's gaze a moment longer than the joke required, and Sadie felt something turn over in her chest, slow and heavy.

She went back to work, but the work changed shape. She had started with one lens and now she found a second pressing against it, the feminist questions from a later page of the packet, about what the marriageable daughters in the novel were actually bargaining with, since the law would hand everything to a male heir. Both lenses, she realized, were asking about the same house from different windows. The women upstairs and the servants downstairs were both trapped in the same economy, though nobody in the drawing room would have put it that way. She wrote a paragraph arguing that the daughters' desperate husband-hunting looked different once you noticed who was ironing the dresses. Then she wrote a second paragraph admitting where the lenses pulled against each other, because they did: the daughters could at least be heard, could speak pages and pages, while the servants stood in doorways holding trays.

Her little brother Noah banged in from the yard, sunburned and thirsty, and Sadie got him water without being asked, ice clattering in the glass, and he drank it beside her chair reading her notes upside down. "Who's the savant?" he asked, pointing at a line where she had written that Austen was no revolutionary.

"That's not how you use it," Sadie said. "A savant is a learned person. Like a scholar. I was being sarcastic about myself for thinking I could judge a whole society from one chapter."

"You're the smartest person I know who can't make toast," Noah said, and stole an apple, and left the glass sweating on her notes. She blotted the ring with her sleeve before it could desiccate into a stain on her only draft.

Near midnight she was still at the table, the kitchen dark except for the lamp over her shoulder, and her conclusion refused to close. She had the trenchant middle section, the part she was proud of, where the empty speech-column did her arguing for her. But the ending kept circling. Was Austen blind to the servants, or was the silence itself a kind of evidence she had left for readers patient enough to count? Sadie could not decide, and the assignment wanted a position. She wrote one sentence she thought was true: the novel does not mention the workers who make its comfort possible, and I do not yet know whether that is a lie it tells or a truth it shows. She read it twice, decided it was honest, and decided that was enough for tonight.

Her mother appeared in the doorway in her robe, hair down, holding two mugs of tea. She set one at Sadie's elbow without a word about the hour, then leaned over and read the last sentence on the page.

"So what's the answer?" her mother asked.

"I don't have one yet," Sadie said, and pulled the mug closer.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
story:
Tyson had promised Ms. Ruiz he would direct the one-act, and he had promised himself he would do it without copying the way Mr. Halloran ran things at the high school, all those years of standing in the dark at the back of the auditorium shouting "Hold, hold, hold" until the cast froze like criminals caught mid-crime. The community theatre had lent him a room above the hardware store on Tuesday and Thursday nights, and for the first week that room was a proscenium like any other: chairs in rows, an imaginary fourth wall, actors facing front. He blocked the whole play that way, scene by scene, sketching arrows in his notebook until the pages looked like diagrams of migrating birds.

Then Marisol, who owned the building, came upstairs with a ring of keys and an apology. The Tuesday sewing circle had doubled in size and she needed the big room back, so the theatre could have the cellar instead, and the cellar, she said apologetically, "is where we do the round things." When Tyson went down to look, he found a low-ceilinged space with chairs stacked in a circle, and it took him a moment to understand what the arrangement meant: the audience would sit on all sides, and everything he had staged for a single viewing angle was suddenly wrong.

"The blocking's dead," said Priya, who was playing the sister, when he explained it. "Every scene, someone's back is to somebody."

He ran the first act anyway, just to see how bad it was, and it was worse than bad. In the argument scene, Devon delivered his entire monologue to the brick wall behind him while Priya and the folding chairs watched his shoulder blades. The chairs' silence was somehow reproachful, four quadrants of empty seats waiting to be treated like people. Tyson stopped the run and stood in the middle of the floor, turning slowly, counting sightlines the way he counted beats in a speech. The play was set on a bare steppe, two siblings arguing over their dead father's land, and he had directed it like a portrait: everyone arranged for one viewer. Down here, there was no one viewer. There were four, or none, depending on how you thought about it, and he was honest enough with himself to admit he didn't yet know which.

"We keep them moving," he said aloud, mostly to himself. "That's the whole trick, isn't it. If they stand still, some section only sees their backs. So we build the scenes in a drift." Priya and Devon looked at each other. "A drift?" "Like weather," Tyson said. "You never stop facing one direction long enough for the other directions to feel ignored."

So they rebuilt the argument. Priya circled the imaginary well; Devon followed; when he accused her of selling the land, she wheeled so the accusation landed across her body and out to the north chairs. It was clumsy at first, blocking invented on the spot, and Tyson made them walk it again and again until the movements stopped feeling imposed. He discovered that a crossing could beguile an audience if the actor took her time, letting each quarter of the room believe she was coming toward them, and he filed that away as a thing he had learned from a cellar and would not have learned from Mr. Halloran's dark auditorium in a hundred years. He was starting to think the old way and this way weren't opposites at all. Both were just answers to the same question, who is watching, and how many of them are there, and what do they deserve to see.

At ten o'clock Marisol came down to lock up and found them still working, the air gray with dust kicked up from the friable edges of the old brick, which crumbled a little under a fingernail and left rust-colored smears on everyone's sleeves. "You found the round," she said, pleased, as though the room itself had been waiting to be used properly again. She watched one scene from the south side, then walked around and watched it again from the north, and told Tyson the second viewing was better, which he suspected was her being kind, and also possibly true.

On the last night before the performance he ran the whole play without stopping, notebook closed in his lap. There were still problems. The final confrontation wanted stillness, two people planted, refusing to move, and the room punished stillness, so he would have to choose between what the moment wanted and what the space demanded, and he did not know yet which was the braver answer. Priya and Devon stood breathless in the middle of the floor, sweat at their temples, waiting for him to say something.

"Same time Thursday?" Devon asked.

Tyson nodded and picked up the keys Marisol had left on the chair by the stairs.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
story:
Amy had taped the paper to the kitchen cabinet at eye level, which meant her mother now knew the mRNA sequence by heart too. AUGCCCUAAAGGCUAC. Below it she'd written her first attempt at decoding: a chain of amino acids she'd assembled with the codon wheel her biology teacher, Ms. Okafor, had handed out before spring break, along with the words "Practice, Ferns, practice."

"Your brother wants dinner," her mother called from the stove, not turning around. "Also that paper has been staring at me all week and I think it's winning."

"It's not supposed to say anything," Amy said. "That's the problem."

The assignment was to translate the mRNA strand into its amino acid chain and bring it to the regional science fair next weekend, where a judge would quiz them. Amy had done it the obvious way: she'd started at the first letter, split the string into triplets, and spun the codon wheel. The wheel had obligingly produced an amino acid for every group of three, because the wheel always did. That was the trap of the wheel. It never said "you're holding me wrong." It just kept converting, letter group by letter group, the way a calculator will happily divide by zero if you've told it to in the right syntax.

Her best friend Priya was on the laptop screen, cross-legged on her own bed with the same paper and a different-colored highlighter. "Okay, so I got proline, stop, arginine, leucine," Priya said. "Which cannot be right, because half the class got the same thing and Ms. Okafor looked at our homework like we'd handed her a wet sock."

"A wet sock," Amy repeated, and wrote it in the margin, because it was the most accurate description of the expression anyone had produced.

"I'm telling you, it's a trick."

"It's not a trick, it's a puzzle. She said puzzles. There was a whole speech." Amy tipped her chair back. There had been a whole speech, in fact, back in February, the day of the assembly where Ms. Okafor had argued against cutting the science budget. Amy remembered it mostly because Ms. Okafor had said the word "hedonism" while describing how the school board treated lab funding, as in they spent it like it was play money for pleasure, not something you amortize over years of students. Amy had looked both words up on the bus home and felt, for one afternoon, like a person who attended board meetings. Then she'd gone back to worrying about the fair.

Priya was intransigent on the subject of trick questions. "She once put a beaker of salt water on a test and asked us to identify it by taste. That woman has no honor."

"She has honor. She has a weird sense of humor. Those aren't the same thing." Amy pulled the paper down off the cabinet and flattened it on the table between her elbows. The sequence sat there, thirteen letters, smug and mute. She read it aloud again, letter by letter, and Priya read along on her copy, and somewhere around the fourth read-through Amy's eye snagged on the first three letters the way a sweater snags on a nail. AUG. She'd translated AUG already. It had come up proline, or arginine, or whatever it was, because she'd started counting from the very first A.

Except. She grabbed her notes from the unit on transcription, flipping past her drawings of RNA polymerase and the doodle she'd done of a ribosome wearing a little hat. Translation, her own handwriting said, underlined twice, begins at the start codon. And beside it, circled in purple: AUG codes for methionine. She'd copied it off the board in March without thinking, the way you copy weather announcements, and it had sat in her binder doing nothing until now.

"Wait," she said. "Say the first three letters."

"A-U-G," said Priya.

"Say what AUG codes for."

There was a pause, the sound of Priya's chair creaking, and then a groan that traveled through the wifi with perfect fidelity. "Methionine. AUG codes for methionine. It's the start codon. We start there."

"We already started there. That's what we did wrong. We started before the start." Amy was already re-splitting the string in her head. If AUG was the signal to begin, then it wasn't just another codon to convert, it was the door. Everything she and Priya had built was a chain that didn't exist, amino acids strung together from a reading that had begun in the wrong place, three letters of pure nonsense at the front and every letter after shifted out of true. The wheel hadn't failed them. They'd asked it the wrong question, and it had answered, because that's what wheels do.

"I'm texting Marcus," Priya said. "He's going to feel so bad. He called me last night and said the assignment was broken and I told him he was broken."

"You told him he was broken?"

"I was tired. It was eleven."

Amy recopied the strand and this time drew the brackets starting at AUG, and the whole thing reshuffled itself into words that were suddenly, obviously words. She read the resulting chain out loud to Priya, twice, and Priya read it back, and somewhere behind her Priya's little brother shouted something about methionine sounding like a place you'd get your taxes done, which, fine, fair.

Her mother set a plate of noodles down at Amy's elbow and studied the paper over her shoulder. "So it was in the right order the whole time," she said.

"It was always in the right order. I was reading from the wrong spot." Amy taped the corrected version back up on the cabinet, right over the old one, so the AUG was at the very top where she could see it.

"Well," her mother said, picking up the fork and pointing it at the paper like a scepter. "Some things you have to start at the beginning to understand. Noodles?"

"Noodles," said Amy, and reached for them.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
story:
Megan arrived at the community studio early, before anyone had unlocked the supply cabinet, and stood in front of the poster of Frida Kahlo's self-portrait with thorn necklace. The instructor, Ms. Oyelaran, had taped it to the easel at the front of the room with a note that read: formal analysis only. Colour, composition, symbolism. No biography.

That was the problem. Megan had spent the whole week reading biography. She had chosen Kahlo for her college application essay because Kahlo was the painter everyone admired at her school, the one whose face appeared on tote bags and mousepads, and Megan had assumed admiration would be enough to carry her through. Now she sat on a paint-spattered stool with a notebook open and no idea how to describe a painting without telling its life story.

"Start with the palette," Ms. Oyelaran said, walking between the easels. "What do you actually see?"

"Green," Megan said. "A green that's almost tropical, but the leaves behind her are darker, like storm-colored." She paused. "The red of the thorns matches the blood at her neck. That's a deliberate echo, isn't it? The same red, one decorative and one violent."

"Say more about where they sit on the canvas."

Megan looked again. The thorns circled the throat, which was also where the little black hummingbird hung, wings outstretched, dead or sleeping. The animal at the center of the composition, the blood at the center of the color scheme, the face above it all perfectly composed, unflinching. She wrote: the painting is organized around the neck. Then she crossed it out and wrote: the painting is organized around endurance, which was closer to something but also worse, more abstract, less seeable.

A boy named Dario, who was taking the class because his mother made him, leaned over her notebook. "That's not formal analysis," he said. "Endurance isn't a color."

"I know that," Megan said, though she hadn't, until he said it.

She went home and did what she always did when a problem refused to break open: she read. Not the glossy biography this time but a plain chronology at the kitchen table while her mother watched television in the other room. On September 17, 1925, when Kahlo was 18, a streetcar crashed into her bus, leaving injuries that caused her pain for the rest of her life. Megan read the sentence twice. Kahlo had been her age. Not the myth, not the tote bag, but an eighteen-year-old on a bus in Mexico City, and then a body that hurt forever after.

The next session, Ms. Oyelaran put the poster back up and asked who wanted to go first. Megan raised her hand before she could reconsider.

"The composition is vertical and frontal, like an icon," she began. "The figure doesn't recede into the leaves; she's pushed forward, almost flat against them, which makes her confrontational. The palette divides cool and warm: the greens and the distant blue behind, against the reds of thorns and blood and the ribbon in her hair. The hummingbird is black, the only true black besides her hair, and it hangs at the axis of the picture." She stopped, looked at her notes, and then closed the notebook. "Symbolically, I read the thorns as a rosary turned punitive. The hummingbird could be freedom, but it's dead, so it's freedom suspended, or it could be a different tradition entirely, and I can't decide which reading the painting supports. It might support both."

"Would you call that a weakness in the analysis?" Ms. Oyelaran asked.

"No," Megan said. "I'd call it honesty. The painting withholds the answer and I don't want to pretend otherwise."

Dario snorted from the back. "So basically you expatiated for five minutes to say you don't know."

"Expounded at length, yes," Megan said. "That's what it's for. Length is how you find the edges of what you know." She had learned that from her father, who used to fill the dinner table with long, patient accounts of plumbing jobs, of pipe fittings and water pressure, and who had died before she could tell him she'd been listening. She thought of him whenever she took something apart slowly.

At the break, Ms. Oyelaran found her by the window. "You mentioned nothing about the accident," she said. "Most students lead with it. They use her pain like a key that opens everything."

Megan turned her coffee cup in her hands. "I almost did. But then I thought, if I make the painting only about what happened to her body, I'm doing the same thing the merchandise does. Turning a person into one wound." She paused. "At the same time, I can't pretend the thorns mean nothing. She was eighteen, my age, when the streetcar hit her bus, and she was in pain the rest of her life. That's in the painting whether I name it or not. I just don't think it's the whole painting."

Ms. Oyelaran nodded slowly, and Megan could not tell whether the nod meant approval or the deliberate withholding of it, another lesson in uncertainty perhaps, or simply a woman deciding it was time to check on the other students.

"Then what do I do with it," Megan asked, "the part I can't leave out and can't use?"

"That," Ms. Oyelaran said, already walking away, "is the critique."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
story:
The morning the chemistry teacher returned their quizzes, Camille got a 61 and folded the paper into her pocket before anyone could see. She had wanted a B in this class all semester, not because she loved chemistry but because her brother had told her that nursing programs counted every science grade twice. After school she took her notebook to the empty chemistry lab, where the late light came through the tall windows and striped the black lab benches, and she set out to learn stoichiometry from the beginning.

The quiz problem had given her fourteen grams of nitrogen gas reacting with excess hydrogen, and asked how many moles of ammonia could form. She had divided by the wrong molar mass, then divided when she should have multiplied, then scribbled it all out and written "I don't know" in the margin. Now she wrote the molar masses along the top of a fresh page, N at 14, and 28 for the nitrogen molecule, because there were two atoms, and she checked that twice. She had begun to habituate herself to checking things twice, the way her grandmother checked the stove, and she found it less humiliating than it sounded.

Her friend Priya found her there at four o'clock, carrying half a sandwich from the cafeteria. "You're doing homework in a lab on a Tuesday," Priya said, dropping her backpack on the stool across the bench.

"I'm doing it over," Camille said. "I got a 61."

Priya tore her sandwich in half and pushed the larger piece across the bench, which was a Priya ordinance, no refusal permitted, and sat down. "Which part?"

"The moles part. Grams going in, moles coming out." Camille turned her notebook so Priya could see the crossed-out wreckage. "There are too many doors between the numbers. I go through the wrong one and end up somewhere that isn't anywhere."

Priya chewed for a while, looking at the page. "Okay," she said. "My mom ran the deli on Ridge Street for six years, before the rent. Watch." She held up the sandwich half. "Say you've got a loaf of bread and a whole tub of turkey. You can make sandwiches until you're out of bread. The turkey's still sitting there, but there's nothing to put it on."

"So the bread stops you."

"The bread stops you." Priya laid four pieces of bread crusts in a line on the bench like a diagram. "It runs out first, and that sets how many sandwiches you can actually make. Doesn't matter how much turkey you've got."

Camille looked at the crusts. Something in her chest loosened slightly, the way it did when a word she'd been pronouncing wrong for years finally got corrected. "Is that a chemistry thing or a deli thing?"

"It's a chemistry thing too, I think. Mr. Okafor said it last week while you were drawing in your margins. He called it the limiting reactant. It's the one that runs out first, and it sets the greatest amount of product a reaction can make." Priya said this the way she repeated her mother's prices, flat and certain, and Camille wrote it down word for word.

She sat with the sentence, turning it over. It was a trenchant little idea, cutting cleaner than anything else in the chapter, and yet she didn't want to just copy it. She wanted to feel where it was true. On her page she set up two reactants, pretended each one alone decided the outcome, and watched the two answers disagree. One of them had to be the smaller one, the one that ran out first, the bread. The other reactant would still be sitting in the pot afterward like the turkey, unused, irrelevant to the count. She did the arithmetic for each line, checking twice, and the two numbers came out different, and she circled the smaller one, and beside it she wrote "this is the cap."

Then she went back to her quiz problem, the one with nitrogen and hydrogen, where the problem had already told her the hydrogen was excess, which she now understood meant it was the turkey. Fourteen grams of nitrogen. She divided by 28 to get moles, wrote the ratio from the balanced equation, carried the units through each line so they canceled like fractions, and arrived at an answer that was small and clean. She checked it twice, then a third time out of pure superstition.

"So did you get it?" Priya asked, gathering her crusts.

"I got an answer that's probably right," Camille said. "The probably is still in there. I won't know until the next quiz whether I actually understand it or whether I just followed the sandwich." She pulled the folded quiz from her pocket and flattened it on the bench next to her new page, the 61 beside the fresh work, and let them sit there together. "But the next quiz is Friday."

"Then you've got two days of bread," Priya said, and Camille laughed and copied the problem onto a clean sheet to do it cold, from nothing, right then, while the light was still in the windows.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
story:
The whiteboard in the library's small study room still held the ghost of a math tutoring session, equations erased but not quite gone, when Brianna commandeered it for her own purposes, wheeling the last marker out of the tray and uncapping it with her teeth. She wrote two headings: OWNERS and WORKERS. Beneath them, she planned to sort the cast of Jane Eyre, because on Monday she had to hand in an essay applying a critical lens, and she had left herself exactly one afternoon.

She had started with the feminist lens, because it came easily. Bertha Mason locked in the attic was not a madwoman so much as an inconvenience being stored. Jane was poor, plain, and female, three conditions that stacked like weights. But when she tried to write the paragraph, it dissolved into generalities, and her notebook margins filled with accusations she could not support. So she had come to the library with the novel, a bag of vending machine pretzels, and the Marxist handout her seminar professor had photocopied, its margins already marked by some previous student in a sullen, contemptuous pencil.

The handout said the bourgeoisie owned the means of production, such as factories and land, while the proletariat owned only its labour and had to sell it for wages. She read it three times, then began sorting. Rochester went under OWNERS, and beneath his name she wrote Thornfield, the land, the mills, whatever else a man like that collected. Mrs. Fairfax, the housekeeper, went under WORKERS. Then she hesitated over Jane herself, and put her on the workers' side too, because a governess sold her labour for wages like anyone else, however nicely she was taught to say it.

"You're taking up the whole board," said a voice from the door. Priya, from her seminar, stood holding a stack of returns for her shift at the circulation desk, her lanyard swinging. "Also, that marker is almost dead. There's a cup of them at the reference desk, the good ones, the fat ones."

"Those are for staff."

"I'm staff." Priya set the cup down anyway, then leaned against the doorframe and read the board upside down with the practiced ease of someone who shelved books all afternoon. "Is that our essay? You're doing the Marxist one?"

"Trying. Keep Rochester as an owner, right? He owns the house, he owns the land."

"He owns basically everyone standing on it," Priya said. "That's the whole thing. The workers don't own anything except their labour, so they have to sell it to him for wages. That's what makes them the other side."

Brianna looked at her sorting. It was almost too tidy. She remembered, suddenly, her grandfather at the kitchen table two summers ago, laying out his union local's newsletter, telling her that a man who works with his hands his whole life can end up owning nothing but the hands. She had thought he was being bitter. Now she recognized the shape of the sentence; somebody had written it down a long time ago, and her grandfather had been quoting it without knowing, the way people quote scripture. "Not exactly nothing," she said out loud, mostly to herself. "The hands."

"The hands are the labour," Priya said. "That's the point. That's the entire inheritance."

Brianna laughed and wrote it in the margin of her draft, then crossed it out, because it wasn't hers. The problem came later, when she reached the end of the novel. Jane inherited money from her uncle, twenty thousand pounds, and married Rochester on equal terms, and Brianna sat with her chin on her fist, marker uncapped, unable to decide where to put her heroine now. Under the feminist lens, the inheritance was liberation; Jane could finally say no to St. John Rivers and mean it. Under the Marxist lens, the inheritance was a promotion into the owning class, and Thornfield had burned, and Rochester had been blinded and maimed, so that the man who owned everything now needed Jane's hands to guide him through his own grounds. "That's not a not a victory," she said, trying the sentence out, and Priya gave her a look. "Litotes," Brianna admitted. "I've been studying rhetorical terms too. It's all leaking into each other."

She wrote both readings on the board in parallel columns and could not make them agree. In one, Jane ended free. In the other, she ended rich, and a rich woman escaping a marriage market was a different kind of escape, the kind you could only make from inside. Brianna did not know which essay to write, or whether the honest essay was the one that held both and admitted it could not resolve them, and the deadline was Monday and the light outside the study room had gone the colour of the library's carpet.

At closing, Priya came back with the key and stood beside her, reading the two columns. Brianna capped the marker, erased OWNERS and WORKERS, and wrote one new heading across the top: WHO BENEFITS. Then, under it, she left a blank space, took a photograph of the board for later, and began gathering her book and her pretzel crumbs.

"You're going to hand in an essay with an empty section?" Priya held the door.

"I'm going to hand in an essay that knows what it doesn't know." Brianna shouldered her bag and followed her out past the darkened computers, past the returned carts, into the parking lot, where Priya's little brother was waiting on the curb with a library card in his teeth and his hand out for her keys.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
story:
Alyssa stood at the bench door with a legal pad full of crossed-out drills and watched the U14 team's passes die on sticks for the fourth time that hour. The weakside winger, Priya, had thrown a seam pass straight through the slot, and a defender's stick had knocked it down like it was nothing. Coach Baranyk had handed her the practice plan last Tuesday with a shrug that said solve it or admit you can't, and so far she had done neither.

"Again," she called, and Priya skated the loop and did it again, and again the puck clattered off the same stick, and Alyssa felt something peevish rise in her chest, an urge to blame the girls for laziness she knew wasn't there. They were passing where the defenders were. That was the whole problem.

She blew the whistle and skated out to the faceoff dot. "Okay. New thing." She set a spare stick flat on the ice like a lying defender, dragged a puck back, and opened her blade so it cradled the puck, then swept through with the blade tilted just so. The puck rose a few inches, sailed flat over the lying stick, and settled onto the tape of her other hand, which she'd extended like a receiver's blade. The girls went quiet.

"What was that?" Priya said.

"Saucer pass," Alyssa said. "It lifts the puck just off the ice so it flies flat over a stick and lands right on the blade."

Nobody asked why it landed flat, and she didn't say. She'd found it the night before in a grainy video at two in the morning, watched the same winger beat the same lying stick forty times, and copied the motion into her own hands in her kitchen with a rolled sock until her mother told her to stop.

That had reminded her of something she'd spent a year trying to forget. Her senior season, the regional semifinal, when the coach had benched her for the entire third period because her passes kept getting picked and the game kept dying at the blue line. She'd sat with her helmet on so nobody could see her face, and afterward, in the parking lot, her father had tried to tell her the coach was an idiot, and she'd said, quietly, that the coach was right. She hadn't known how to fix it either. Nobody had shown her that there was a fix.

She lined the girls up in three rows. First drill: partner passing over a stationary stick, no movement, just the lift and the landing. Half the saucers wobbled and slapped down like thrown pancakes. "Softer hands," she said, skating the row. "You're shoveling it. You're not trying to launch it." Priya's first three failed; her fourth floated over the stick and sat down on her partner's blade without a bounce, and Priya looked up like she'd performed a magic trick on herself.

Second drill, she made it game-speed: a chaser with a stick active in the passing lane, forced decisions. This was where it got messy, and where she caught herself doing the thing she disliked most in coaches, treating the drill like a machine that would produce output if she just calibrated the inputs correctly, some clean little technocracy of cones and reps. When the passes failed now, it wasn't mechanics failing. It was ten different girls deciding, in half a second, whether to try the thing they'd learned an hour ago or the safe thing they'd done for years. That wasn't a calibration problem. She stopped the drill and pulled Priya aside.

"When the stick's in the lane, you don't have time to choose," Alyssa said. "So choose now. Saucer every seam pass in this drill, even the bad ones."

"Even if they don't work?"

"Especially if they don't work."

Priya looked at her for a second, and Alyssa understood the look, because she'd given it to a bench once. Then the drill restarted, and for two minutes it was ugly, saucers sailing wide, one flipping end over end into the corner, a girl named Drea maligning the whole drill under her breath, loud enough to be heard, which was probably the point. Then Priya took a pass at the blue line with a defender's stick slicing across the seam, and without hesitating she opened her blade and floated the puck over it, flat, soft, onto Derra's tape at the far post, and Derra one-timed it in before the goalie's knees were set.

The rink went loud. Baranyk tapped the glass once with a knuckle, which from him was a parade. Alyssa wrote nothing on the legal pad. She knew what she'd seen, and she also knew what she didn't know yet: whether it would survive an actual game on Sunday, whether one drilled skill could change a team or only decorate it, whether the coach who had benched her could have been shown this same thing and simply never was. She could hold both of those at once. On the next rep, Priya did it again, and this time the defender lifted her stick to knock it down, and the puck dropped flat onto Derra's blade anyway, and Derra buried it, and Priya turned toward the bench with her mouth open.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
story:
Sienna arrived at the tutoring centre with a quiz folded into quarters in her back pocket, which she kept patting like a wallet she expected to be stolen. The centre smelled of dry-erase markers and the stale cheer of motivational posters, one of which maligned procrastination in Comic Sans, an accusation Sienna found rich coming from a laminated piece of paper. She dropped her bag on the chair beside Marcus, who was already there, headphones around his neck, workbook open to a page he was clearly pretending to have finished.

"Five out of ten," she said, laying the quiz flat between them. "On a question I knew how to do."

Marcus leaned over it. The question asked for the largest value of a function on an interval from zero to six, and Sienna's work marched down the page in tidy columns: differentiate, set the derivative equal to zero, solve, declare victory. The marker's red comment ran along the top like a small obstreperous banner: "You found the critical point. Did you check the whole interval?"

"I found the critical point," Sienna said. "That's the whole assignment. That's the treasure. I dug up the treasure."

"You dug up a treasure," Marcus said. "There might be a bigger treasure at the edge of the map."

She threw a foam dart at him, and it bounced off the whiteboard behind his head, and Priya at the next table said "Hey" without looking up, the way she always did, a syllable that functioned as both warning and greeting.

The two of them worked the problem again on the big board while Priya pretended not to watch and watched the whole time. Sienna differentiated the polynomial, set the thing equal to zero, and got x equals four, sitting squarely inside the interval. She computed the function's value there, wrote it in a box, and was reaching for the marker cap when Priya finally abandoned her pretense.

"What's the function at six?" Priya asked.

"Why does it matter at six? Six is the edge. Nothing happens at the edge."

"Then why did they bother telling you zero to six?"

Sienna stood with the marker uncapped, which was itself a small suspense, because the cap was in her other hand and she had a history of losing it under tables. In seventh grade, on a museum trip, she had spent forty minutes outside the planetarium arguing with a classmate about whether Pluto had been treated fairly, whether demoting a planet was like demoting a kid to the back row, and she remembered the moment her own argument turned on her: if size mattered, then Pluto was out, and if belonging mattered, then Pluto was in, and she could not have both. She had hated that feeling at twelve. She recognized it now, the same tipping point, the sensation of a position starting to slide.

She calculated the function at six, the far endpoint. It was larger than her critical point's value. She calculated it at zero too, for completeness, and it was smaller. She wrote the six's value in a second box, beside the first, and looked at them together for a moment, the way you look at two photos of the same person taken on different days.

"So the biggest value isn't even where the derivative is zero," she said slowly. "It's at the end. The derivative isn't zero there, it's just... the edge."

"The map has edges," Marcus said. "Treasures can be at the edge of the map."

"On a closed interval," Priya said, in her quiz-show voice, "the largest value can occur at an endpoint where the derivative isn't zero, so you have to check the endpoints too." Then she ruined the effect by adding, "That's the whole fact, you can put that in your essay," and went back to her worksheet as though she had not spoken.

Sienna rewrote the question's answer with the endpoint's value, then wrote, underneath, an apology to herself in the margin: "You were not wrong, you were incomplete." She looked at it and decided incomplete was still a kind of wrong, but a wrong you could fix with one more calculation, which made it, in her private taxonomy, the least tragic stratum of wrongness, far above the wrongs you couldn't arithmetic your way out of.

At the next session she brought a new quiz, this one nine out of ten, and a mark deducted for arithmetic, not ideas. She slid it across to Marcus. "A treasure at the edge of the map," she said, "that I buried myself, apparently."

"Dig it up," he said, and handed her the marker.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
story:
Jasmine spread the print across the picnic table so the wind could not take it, weighting the corners with her mother's old canning jars. The assignment sheet lay beside it, folded into eighths from being carried in her back pocket all week: five hundred words of formal analysis, color, composition, symbolism, due Monday. She had been admitted early to the state university with a scholarship conditional on passing this art history course, and the professor had already returned her first essay with a single comment in red ink: "Description is not analysis. Say why."

The print showed Frida Kahlo staring out from a wall of leaves, a thorn necklace cutting into her neck, a small black bird hanging dead at her throat. Jasmine had chosen it because it was famous and because she assumed it would be easy, that she could write about the green against the skin, the flat frontal pose, the blood at the thorns' points, and be finished by dinner. She had written one paragraph in three days. Every sentence she produced sounded like a caption, and she had begun to suspect that "why" was a door she did not have a key to.

Her grandmother came out with two glasses of horchata and set one down on the table's far edge, away from the jars. She looked at the print for a long moment before she sat. "Mi Frida," she said. "Your mother had this on a postcard in college. She taped it over her desk until the tape yellowed."

Jasmine pulled the assignment sheet closer, glad for the company but braced against another interruption. "I have to critique it formally," she said. "Not just say I like it. Like, the composition is symmetrical, she's centered, the animals flank her, the monkey on one shoulder and the cat on the other. And the color is mostly green with her face like an island in the middle. That's what I have so far."

"That's a list," her grandmother said, not unkindly.

"I know." Jasmine tapped the bird hanging from the thorn necklace, its wings folded, its body still. "And I don't even know what this is. Is it just decoration? Some surrealism thing? The professor said symbolism counts as formal analysis if you connect it to the composition, but I can't connect something I don't understand."

Her grandmother leaned over the print, squinting. "Ah, el colibrí," she said. "In Mexico, a dead hummingbird hanging like that is a charm for luck in love." She straightened up and sipped her horchata as though she had remarked on the weather.

Jasmine wrote the sentence down before the wind could take that too. A charm for luck. She looked at the painting again and felt something shift, sedimentary layers she had been staring past suddenly separating into distinct strata: the black bird against the white of the blouse, the thorns drawing blood, the expression that was neither smiling nor suffering but holding both at once. If the dead bird was meant to bring luck in love, then the painting was about wanting, and everything arranged around that want. The monkeys and cats in Mexican folk tradition, the leafy background pressing in like a crowded room, the symmetry that made her look composed, staged, deliberate, while the thorns said otherwise.

"Why a dead one, though?" Jasmine asked. "Why not a live hummingbird? That seems backwards."

Her grandmother shrugged, a gesture that contained whole decades. "You want luck because you need it. Nobody carries a charm for something they already have." She picked up the empty glass and went back inside, leaving Jasmine with the smell of cinnamon and the print and the afternoon light moving across the table.

Jasmine opened her notebook and began again from scratch. She wrote about the diagonal of the bird against the horizontal of the necklace, about how Kahlo placed the charm at the exact center of the portrait, over her heart but at her throat, so that wanting and speaking occupied the same spot. She wrote that the lushness of the background greens was not backdrop but pressure, a kind of symbiosis between the figure and the foliage that never settled into comfort, since the leaves behind her were beautiful and also dense enough to swallow a person. She did not pretend certainty. She wrote one sentence admitting that she could not tell whether Kahlo believed in the charm or was mocking her own hope, and she left it in, because the professor's "why" felt like a question with more than one true answer.

When she finished drafting, the sun had dropped behind the fence and the jars threw long shadows across Kahlo's face. The essay was not what she would have written a week ago, when she thought analysis meant listing what she saw. It had cost her three days and one ordinary conversation, and it still contained a paragraph she was unsure of, a claim she had written "possibly" in front of and then crossed out and then written again. She read the last line aloud to the empty yard, testing it against the painting, and found that it held. Then she folded the print with more care than it probably needed, carried it inside, and set it on her desk where the tape could find it in the morning.

activity: getting a first part-time job
story:
The hiring table at Camp Winnowick sat under a canopy that smelled like sunscreen and melted plastic, and Alex signed his name beside a wage line that read $7.25. He was eighteen, he had a working car, and forty hours a week at seven twenty-five still felt like a kind of adult arrival. He did the math on the drive home, twice, and decided the number was enough for gas and a portion of tuition that could only be described as symbolic.

Marcus, who had been his bunkmate for three summers before they both aged into staff, worked at a camp twenty minutes east, across the state line. They had made a ritual of texting after their days ended, comparing crafts ruined and children lost and found, and by the second Friday Marcus sent a photograph of his first paycheck stub. Alex opened his own stub, laid the phones side by side on his hood, and understood immediately that something was off, though it took him another minute to see that the difference was in the rate, not the hours.

"You get ten fifty," Alex said into the phone. "For the same job."

"CPR certification and everything," Marcus said, with a satisfaction that traveled the distance intact. "Same lake. Technically the same river."

Alex sat on the hood and looked at the stubs. Seven twenty-five versus ten fifty, identical jobs, identical sunscreen, twenty minutes of highway between them. It offended some instinct of proportion. He had assumed, without ever examining the assumption, that a job was a job and the number attached to it was the number, arrived at by some adult process in a distant office, the way gravity was arrived at.

At lunch on Monday he asked Deshawn, the program director, whether the camp ever paid more. Deshawn was spraying down the picnic tables with a hose and did not turn around. "We pay minimum," he said. "Legal minimum. You want more, talk to the state, not to me." Then, as though the hose had reminded him, he added, "Other side of the river, they've got their own minimum. Ours is the federal one."

Alex looked it up on his break, sitting on an overturned canoe with his phone cupped against the glare. The federal minimum wage was $7.25 an hour, and it had been $7.25 since July 24, 2009. Fourteen years. He read the date twice, waiting for it to transfigure into something else, a typo, a footnote, some detail that would make the number sit differently in his stomach. It did not. Many states and cities, the page went on, set their own higher minimums, which was why Marcus's camp paid ten fifty and his did not, though the page offered no judgment on this, being a page.

He spent the afternoon lifeguarding the shallow end, where the water was waist-high and the danger was mostly social. His co-counselor Priya argued with a nine-year-old about whether a frog counted as a lake animal or a land animal that visited, and Alex found himself weighing in on the frog's side purely for the pleasure of the argument. Later, drying off, he tried to sort out what he actually thought. Marcus's camp paid better, so the rational move was to apply there next summer, or even now, mid-season. But he knew these kids, knew which one hid during cleanup and which one cried at pickup on Thursdays, and the thought of handing that knowledge to a stranger for three dollars and a quarter an hour felt, in a way he couldn't quite defend, like selling something that wasn't his.

"You're doing the face," Priya said, folding her towel into a square of aggressive precision.

"I'm doing math."

"You're doing the face you do when you think the world is supposed to be consistent." She slung the towel over her shoulder. "It's not, by the way. Consistent. I checked."

"That's very comforting."

"I'm not here to comfort you. I'm here for the paddle boats."

He laughed, and the laugh loosened something. He was aware that he could hold both things: that the wage was unfair in a way a state line shouldn't be able to produce, and that he might still choose to stay, and that choosing to stay would be a choice and not simply inertia, though he couldn't yet say which it was. His father would call the whole thing simple economics and be wrong in the confident tone of a man who had never needed the money. His brother would call it an outrage and be wrong in a different direction, turning seven twenty-five into a symbol rather than a paycheck. Alex suspected the truth was more parochial than either of them wanted: two camps, one river, a number set by people who had never sprayed down these picnic tables. And he suspected that his own refusal to reduce it further was either wisdom or pedantry, and that he wouldn't know which for years.

He drove home with the windows down, the stub still folded in his pocket. At the state line, where the highway signs changed color without ceremony, he slowed down and looked left, toward the other camp, its water tower just visible past the trees. Then he put his foot back on the gas and crossed.

story:
The textbook had followed him to his grandfather's house in its own way, which is to say his mother had packed it, wrapped in a grocery bag between his boots and his winter coat, as though calculus were a thing he might forget on purpose. He found it the first evening while unpacking, along with a note in her looping hand: "Placement exam is the last Friday of August. This is not a punishment. This is me loving you in an annoying way. There is soup in the blue jar." He read it twice, then folded it into the back cover, where it would stay all week.

The house sat at the edge of town where the streets gave up and the boreal forest began, spruce and birch running north without interruption. His grandfather had lived alone in it since March, and the place showed the arithmetic of that: one chair angled at the window, one mug, one plate in the drying rack, but the whole greenhouse out back still full of August tomatoes nobody was eating fast enough.

"So you're doing the mathematics," his grandfather said the next morning, setting down coffee Raphael hadn't asked for. "In my day we did it with a slide rule and a certain amount of prayer." He proselytized about most subjects, compost especially, and the decline of handwriting, and the superiority of rain barrels over municipal water, but mathematics he treated more gently, the way he talked about weather or old friends.

Raphael spread the book on the kitchen table under the window's flat gray light. Chapter three was derivatives of polynomials, and he could feel the placement exam on the far side of it like a border crossing. He worked the rules without believing them: bring the exponent down, subtract one. The notation was the part that snagged him. The book wrote the derivative as dy over dx, stacked like an honest fraction, and yet the chapter insisted it wasn't one. He flipped backward through the pages looking for whoever had decided this and found the answer buried in a footnote smaller than the copyright information. The notation dy/dx came from Gottfried Leibniz, and it was still standard in mathematics today. Three hundred years of students copying a fraction that wasn't a fraction from a man none of them had heard of.

"Why does it look like that if it's not one?" his grandfather asked, reading over his shoulder with his glasses pushed up into his hair.

"Leibniz wrote it that way," Raphael said. "It's still how everybody writes it. I don't know why it stuck." He said it plainly, because he didn't, and something about admitting that steadied him. The notation was a kind of inheritance, like the soup jar, like the house itself, useful without being understood.

That afternoon his grandfather stood him in front of the garden with a coil of wire fencing and a problem that had apparently been waiting for him. Forty meters of mesh, salvaged when the neighbor tore down his run, and a patch of ground between the greenhouse and the tree line where the deer had stopped bothering to come. "I want the pen for next spring's chickens," his grandfather said. "Biggest area you can get me. And don't say a square because it looks nice."

Raphael almost did say a square, and then caught himself, and went inside for his notebook. If one side was x, the opposite side was x, and the two remaining sides together were forty minus two x, so each was twenty minus x. Area equaled x times the quantity twenty minus x, which expanded to twenty x minus x squared. He took the derivative, twenty minus two x, the exponent coming down like the textbook said it would, set it equal to zero, and got x equals ten. A square, ten by ten, one hundred square meters, and he hadn't guessed it, he had located the maximum, the exact point where growth on one side stopped paying for what it cost on the other. He carried the notebook outside like a verdict.

His grandfather studied the numbers, then laughed, a sound Raphael hadn't heard since the funeral and hadn't known the house still contained. He walked Raphael to the far corner of the garden, past the greenhouse, and stopped at a line of standing stones with rotting posts between them. "Your grandmother's goose pen," he said. "Forty years ago. She had the same forty meters, more or less." He toed the ground and began pacing it out, boot by boot, along the old line. Ten meters one way, ten the other. A square, worn into the grass before Raphael was born.

"It's the same answer," Raphael said. "She got the same answer."

"She didn't do any mathematics," his grandfather said. "She stood here and looked at it and moved sticks around for a day." He planted his heel at what must have been the corner post and tapped the notebook in Raphael's hand. "So which of you is the smarter one?"

Raphael looked at the rectangle of cropped grass, at his own numbers, at the stones that had been quietly correct the whole time, and honestly did not know. The exam was still coming, the fraction that wasn't a fraction still waited on its page, and he had four more days of his grandfather's coffee to figure out what it meant that the same maximum could be reached by a dead woman with sticks. "I'll stake the corners," he said, and went to get the mallet.

story:
The screen door announced Owen before he reached the kitchen, and his grandfather looked up from a crossword with the mild expectation of someone who had been waiting all morning without admitting it. Owen set his laptop on the table beside the fruit bowl and said he had to finish a lab before Monday. He was building a class in Java, his first real one, with private fields and getter methods, and then tests to prove it worked. His grandfather, retired from forty years of managing other people's money, pushed the crossword aside and asked what a private field was, exactly.

"Private means nobody outside the class can touch it," Owen said. "They have to ask. You write a getter, like getBalance, and it hands the value back." He typed while he talked, building a small class called Account with one field, a double named balance, and a getter so plain it felt almost embarrassing to write. His grandfather watched the words appear and said it sounded sensible. "A man who held your money had what the law called a fiduciary duty," he said. "Everything in the open, nothing moved without a reason. Your getter is the same idea. A door with a bell on it." Owen said that was roughly it, though he suspected the comparison flattered the code.

The tests came next. Their instructor had insisted on JUnit, and had insisted, twice, that tests be written before anyone was comfortable. Owen wrote a line that created an Account with a starting balance of one hundred, then called assertEquals and gave it two numbers. He ran the test, and it failed. The failure message said the test expected 100.0 but the actual value was 50.0. He stared at it for a long moment, because he had put 50.0 in the constructor, or thought he had, and the message was telling him something about his own intentions that didn't match his memory of them.

He checked the constructor. He checked the getter. He reread the field declaration, which sat there, private and impervious, refusing to explain anything. "It says it expected a hundred," he told his grandfather, "but I never typed a hundred anywhere." His grandfather leaned in, reading the red text on the screen the way he might read a discrepancy in an old ledger, without panic, with only the patience of a man who had chased a misplaced decimal across many afternoons. He did not offer a theory. He asked where the two numbers in the test line had come from.

Owen looked at the line again. assertEquals, then 50.0, then account.getBalance(). He had put the value he wanted first and the method call second, the way you'd read a sentence, and it had seemed natural, the naturalness of it was the problem. He opened the JUnit documentation on his phone and read it twice. assertEquals takes the expected value first and the actual value second. He had them swapped. The message had been reporting his own argument back to him, faithful and useless, the whole time.

"Wait," he said slowly. "So the number it calls expected is just the first thing I gave it. It's not judging anything. It's repeating." He swapped the arguments so the expected value came first and the actual value came second, ran the test again, and watched it pass, the bar going green with a small, unsatisfying click. He sat back. Part of him wanted to denigrate the whole framework, to call it a trap for people who read left to right, but that wasn't fair either, and he knew it wasn't fair, and he was old enough now to notice himself knowing it. The order wasn't a trick. It was a convention, like driving on a particular side of the road, wrong only for someone who hadn't learned it yet.

Still, he didn't like how long it had taken him, and he didn't like that even now, with the green bar in front of him, he couldn't say he fully understood why the convention was that way and not the other. He could describe it. He could follow it. Whether he'd have designed it the same, he honestly didn't know. He said so, out loud, more to the fruit bowl than to anyone, and his grandfather nodded as though this were the most ordinary report in the world. "Most of what I knew about money was like that at first," he said. "You follow the rule before you trust it. Sometimes you never get to the trusting part, and you follow it anyway."

Owen wrote a second test, deliberately, with the expected value first and the actual value second, then a third that asked the getter for a value he'd never set, just to see what the message would say when the class had nothing to hide. His grandfather had gone back to the crossword but looked over at each run of the tests, at the green bars accumulating. "Eleven across," he said eventually. "Seven letters, sounds like it means careless, actually means willing to be answerable." Owen glanced at the clue, then at his three passing tests lined up beside the fruit bowl. "Accountable," he said.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
story:
The nurse's station at Camp Wren Lake smelled of chlorine and adhesive tape, and Aiden had spent the better part of July avoiding it, until the day the health instructor, a wiry college senior named Ro, assigned everyone to the blood pressure station. Aiden was at camp on a science scholarship that required a health literacy project, and he had chosen it partly to burnish his application, partly because his mother had said, in her offhand way, that he might finally learn something practical instead of calculus.

Ro handed out cuffs and a laminated card and then wandered off to argue with the lifeguard about the chlorine levels, which meant the campers taught themselves. Aiden's partner was a girl named Priya who wore a whistle she never used, an affectation she defended by saying it made people take her seriously. She pumped the cuff on Aiden's arm while he winced, and they read the numbers together, then swapped. After the third practice, Priya picked up the card and frowned.

"Listen to this," she said. "Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 1 hypertension means a systolic reading of 130 to 139 or a diastolic reading of 80 to 89." She squinted at the card. "That's a lot lower than I thought."

Aiden felt something shift in his chest, quiet and unwelcome. Two weeks before camp, he had sat at his grandfather's kitchen table while the old man slept in his chair, and he had found the home monitor log on the counter, a spiral notebook with dates and numbers in his grandfather's cramped hand. 132 over 84. 136 over 82. 134 over 87. Page after page of it, all summer, all spring. Aiden had looked at those numbers and thought they looked like nothing, like the kind of numbers a machine prints to seem busy. He had closed the notebook and gone out to the dock, insouciant about the whole thing, and when his grandfather woke and asked what he'd been doing, Aiden said looking for the good spoons.

He had not thought about it since. Now the laminated card sat in his hand under the fluorescent light, and every one of those readings fell inside the range Priya had just read aloud. He turned the card over, as though the back might soften the front. It listed diet and exercise in cheerful bullet points, the kinds of changes he could picture his grandfather making for exactly one week, the week after his hip surgery, before the recliner won.

"Your turn to read mine," Priya said, and he did, mechanically, wrapping the cuff around her arm and listening for the pulse to vanish and return. His own readings were fine, 118 over 74, which he had expected and which now struck him as a kind of luck rather than a virtue. He thought about his grandfather's cooking, the salt on everything, the butter as a food group, the walks that had shortened from around the block to around the kitchen. He also thought about the man's stubbornness, his refusal to see a doctor since Aiden's grandmother died, and the possibility that telling him what the numbers meant would start a fight Aiden would lose.

But he kept thinking about a distinction Priya had stumbled into without noticing. Systolic or diastolic. Either one alone was enough, the card said, with that flat authority of medical print. It didn't require both. It didn't require certainty, or a family history, or Aiden's opinion of whether his grandfather looked healthy sitting in that chair. The guideline made a decision out of a threshold, and thresholds were unglamorous, but they were decisions made by someone who did not have to sit across from the man at breakfast.

That evening, after the campfire, Aiden stood by the pay phone outside the canteen, the one nobody used anymore, coins in his palm from the office. He had decided to call, and then, standing there, he began composing what he would say and found that every version sounded like a diagnosis, like he was the one with the laminated card. Maybe he would just ask about the log. Maybe he would mention the readings and let his grandfather reach the conclusion himself, or refuse to. Priya came out of the canteen with a popsicle and watched him holding the receiver without dialing.

"You're going to use that thing or just burnish it?" she said.

Aiden fed in the coins and dialed the number he had known since he was six, and while it rang, he looked at the dark lake and rehearsed nothing at all. When his grandfather answered, his voice thick with sleep, Aiden said, "Hi, it's me. Do you still have that notebook by the coffee maker?"

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
story:
The retake was scheduled for Thursday, which gave Jessica three days to understand something she had spent two weeks memorizing without understanding. She had failed the unit quiz on transcription and translation by four points, and Mrs. Okonkwo had a rule she applied without exception: to retake anything, you had to show up to Tuesday lab and work the material with your hands. So Jessica signed the equipment waiver on Monday, the one that promised to indemnify the school against any damage she might do to a microscope she had no intention of touching, and came in after last period with her failed quiz folded in her back pocket.

Marcus was already at the long counter, arranging paper strips. He'd passed the quiz, barely, and had agreed to help because Jessica had driven him to the dentist in October and he considered the debt unpaid. "Okay," he said. "I printed the sequence again. Same one from the quiz. We're going to build it."

"Build it."

"Don't be facetious. Physically build it. Paper for the DNA, paper for the RNA, then the amino acids at the end. Mrs. Okonkwo says if you can build it, you can explain it, and if you can explain it, you actually have it."

The DNA strand was written across the top of the handout in a string of letters, and Jessica's job was to write out the RNA that would be read off it. This was transcription, the part she'd missed entirely on the quiz. She worked slowly, matching each letter to its partner, and produced a strip she was almost proud of. She slid it across the counter.

Marcus looked at it for a long moment, then longer, then turned it around so it faced her. "You wrote T."

"That's the letter that goes there."

"That's the letter that goes in DNA." He tapped the strip. "This is RNA. Look at your strip. You've got a U at position four and a T at position nine. You're not even wrong consistently."

Jessica stared at the two letters, sitting in the same strip like they belonged together. She flipped back through her quiz, to the question worth six points, and found the same thing: a strand of RNA with a T sitting in the middle of it like a stone in a river. Somewhere in her notes was the fact, copied off the board in blue pen, and she found it and read it and understood, for the first time, that she had read it a dozen times before without ever letting it change what her hand did. In the DNA, adenine went with thymine and guanine went with cytosine. In the RNA, uracil took the place of thymine. Same job, different letter.

"So it's not that RNA has its own separate rules," she said slowly. "It's the same pairing, adenine still goes with the same partner, except the partner has a different name."

"If you want to get philosophical about it," Marcus said, "the RNA spelling is a different word for the same thing. Like how the Greeks had one word, logos, that meant both the word and the reason behind it. The cell says the same thing in a different language."

"That's the most you've ever said in lab."

"I'm indemnified against embarrassment. I signed the waiver."

She wrote the strip out again, this time watching her own hand, and the habit of the T was stronger than she expected, like a path her pencil knew better than she did. At position eleven she caught herself mid-letter, the vertical stroke of a T already down, and curved the crossbar away and up into a U. It looked like a small wound in the letter. She kept going. At the end she had a clean strip, and Marcus handed her the codon chart, and she translated the RNA into its amino acids one triplet at a time, reading, matching, writing, and it felt less like memory than like following a sentence whose grammar she finally knew.

On Thursday she sat the retake and finished with eleven minutes left, and when Mrs. Okonkwo handed back the folded page on Friday, Jessica saw the grade before she'd fully unfolded it, a number high enough that she read it twice. She walked out into the corridor holding it, and found Marcus at the water fountain.

"Let me see," he said, and took the page, and his face did something complicated. "Huh."

"What."

"Nothing. It's just, that's two points higher than mine." He handed it back and started walking. "So Thursday, when I'm retaking it, you're building the strips with me, right? Since we're even now."

"Even? I drove you to the dentist."

"That was for a cleaning. This is for a grade. Different currency entirely." He pushed through the lab door and pointed at the counter where the paper strips still lay from Tuesday. "Start with the DNA. And this time, don't let me write a single T in the RNA."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
story:
The reading nook was really just the window seat with a lamp clipped to the curtain rod, but Kaitlyn had defended it with such ferocity over the years that her brother Dex now knocked before entering, even though it was technically a hallway. Tonight she had the whole thing to herself: two pillows, a granola bar, and a paperback of Huckleberry Finn with a crack down its spine like a fault line.

Mrs. Amaro's assignment sheet sat beside her, one question underlined twice in green: Who is telling you this story, and can you trust the telling? Kaitlyn had written a first answer in class, "Yes, Huck tells the truth," and Mrs. Amaro had circled it and written, "Interesting. Test it." Two words, and now Kaitlyn had spent forty minutes in the window seat feeling like she'd been handed a locked box with the key sold separately.

She read the scene where Huck attends his own funeral. Huck hides in the loft of the church, watching the townspeople weep over the boy they believe is drowned, and reports it all with mild surprise and considerable satisfaction at the crowd turnout. Kaitlyn caught herself laughing out loud, then covered her mouth, then laughed again. The parson "made a grand and gorgeous" speech, Huck said, and the whole thing worked, the mourning worked, the spectacle worked, and Huck took it at face value, pleased that so many people had cared about him and slightly proud of the quality of the sermon.

Dex appeared at the edge of the nook with a hiking guide in one hand. "Can I sit? I need to parametrize the route before Saturday, and the light in here is objectively better than my room." He was plotting their father's birthday hike on graph paper, deciding which variables mattered, distance versus elevation versus how badly Dad's knees disliked steep descents. The guide promised a stretch of montane forest near the top, which Dex pronounced "mon-TANE" until Kaitlyn corrected him and he said the wrong pronunciation again on purpose, twice.

"Why is that funny?" Dex asked, nodding at the book, because she was grinning at it like it had told her a secret.

"That's what I'm trying to figure out." She showed him the page. "He's at his own funeral. He thinks it's a pretty good funeral. He's complimenting the sermon."

Dex read, slowly, mouthing some of it. "He doesn't know it's funny," he said finally.

Kaitlyn sat up so fast the lamp swung. "That's it. He doesn't know. That's why it's funny." She flipped backward through chapters, hunting for the scene where Jim grieves over his daughter, slapped once for not obeying, before Huck understood she couldn't hear; Huck recorded it plainly, without commentary, and she had read right past it last week. "He's not lying to me. He tells everything exactly like it happened. He just doesn't understand what he's looking at."

"Sounds like a problem."

"It's the opposite of a problem. It's the whole engine." She pulled her notebook over and wrote, in her fast downhill handwriting, He reports honestly but misunderstands, so I see more than he does. Then, underneath: that's why the funeral works. Then she remembered Mrs. Amaro's green underline and stopped, pencil hovering. Trust was the wrong frame, maybe. Huck was trustworthy in one direction and blind in another, and the book trusted the reader to stand somewhere the narrator couldn't, which felt less like being deceived and more like being handed a second pair of eyes. She wrote that down too, then crossed out half of it because it sounded like a fortune cookie.

"So what do you call it?" Dex asked, squinting at her notes. "When the narrator's honest but clueless?"

"A naive narrator," Kaitlyn said. "That's the term. At least I think that's the term. Mrs. Amaro will tell me Monday." She reached over and stole his graph paper, added a vertical axis, and labeled it "how much Huck understands," then drew a line starting near the floor. "But here's the thing, this line moves. Chapter thirty-one Huck is not chapter one Huck. If I draw it like it's flat, I'm doing the same thing I accused the book of, pretending a person is one number."

Dex took his graph paper back with dignity. "That's the deepest thing anyone has ever done to my hike plan. You owe me reparation." He held out his palm, and she paid him the second half of the granola bar, which he ate while she reread the funeral scene once more, pencil behind her ear, the montane route forgotten between them, the window going dark over the street.

"Chapter one Huck," she murmured, turning back to the beginning, "let's see where you started."

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and old carpet, because Laurie's father had laid down a rug out here years ago and then never actually parked the car on it. Laurie used the garage as her practice room, which meant the upright piano lived between the snowblower and a shelf of paint cans, and her phone lay face up on the bench so she could see when Theo finally texted back.

She had a deadline, of sorts. Her piano teacher had offered her twenty dollars, an honorarium she pronounced carefully to herself as though it made her a professional, to prepare a short talk for the younger students on Saturday about the Mozart K. 545 first movement. The talk required her to mark the score: exposition, development, recapitulation, brackets in the margins, the whole architecture laid bare.

Laurie had started confidently. The exposition announced itself, first theme in C, second theme in G, and she drew her bracket with the good pencil, the one her father did not use for marking lumber. The development she found by ear before she found it on paper, that stretch where Mozart wandered off through minor keys like someone checking every drawer in the house for keys that weren't there. Then the first theme returned, bright and innocent in C, and she wrote recapitulation and drew the closing bracket where the music seemed to settle.

Except the music didn't settle. Four more measures went by, and the right hand kept hammering C and G, insisting, redundant, almost smug, and Laurie's brackets ended before the page did.

She played the passage three times. Theo, who took theory at the conservatory prep program and wore this fact lightly the way other people wore cologne, had texted her half an hour ago that marking sonata form was "basically plumbing, you follow the pipes." She had replied that he was the kind of person who thought that was a compliment, and now she regretted it slightly, because she needed him.

"There's an extra bit at the end," she typed. "After the recap. What is it."

She waited. To look busy she played the last page again, and her father put his head in through the side door, holding a sandwich. "You've played the ending six times."

"It's not the ending. That's the problem."

He considered this the way he considered most things she said about music, with affection and complete incomprehension, then left her to it. The phone buzzed.

"Coda," Theo wrote. Then, because he was Theo: "It's optional. Comes after the recapitulation. Hammers the home key so the movement can actually end. You're welcome."

Laurie looked at the four extra measures. C, then G, then C again, the harmony as flat and final as an alluvial plain, everything deposited in the same place, layer on layer, until the river had nowhere left to go. She penciled a small bracket and wrote coda, and then sat back and looked at the whole marked page.

What bothered her was that she had almost dismissed those measures as filler. She had wanted the form to be a clean diagram, three boxes, done, and the coda had sat outside her boxes being smug about its optionality. But now that she could see it, she couldn't unsee it: the movement needed the extra weight, or at least Mozart had thought so, and there was a difference between needing and choosing that she couldn't quite close. Maybe some movements ended when their material ended, and maybe some had to be persuaded.

She tried writing a sentence for the talk: "The coda is a closing section after the recapitulation, optional, reinforcing the home key to bring the movement to an end." It read like a Wikipedia page written by a metronome. She crossed it out and tried again: "Sometimes the music isn't finished when the form is." Better, though possibly she would regret it in front of eleven-year-olds on Saturday.

Her phone buzzed once more. "Also," Theo said, "whatever you do don't stigmatize the coda in your talk, the little kids will start thinking endings are embarrassing."

She typed "nobody is stigmatizing anything" and put the phone face down on the rug. Then she played the movement through from the top, and when she reached the last four measures she played them louder than she ever had, left hand and right, C and G, the whole garage rattling faintly with it, paint cans buzzing on their shelf like they wanted to applaud.
